entry.title: feat(es): the conjugation engine — 27 patterns, and the exceptions cl…
entry.content:
feat(es): the conjugation engine — 27 patterns, and the exceptions clustered by what changed

Phase 6's generator. Derived, never generated: every fact comes from
lib/data/es-grammar.json, which every Spanish learner already downloads for the
grammar note in the word popup, so a table of conjugation facts would be a second
record of what the first already says and would drift the moment either was
rebuilt. No build script, no new data file. 1,259 verbs analysed end to end in
246 ms, once, behind a lazy import that has already happened.

THE DIFFING ENGINE CUTS AT A KNOWN BOUNDARY. The obvious move is to compare the
two whole strings and call the difference the stem, and it is wrong in a way that
survives testing: `pensa` against `piensa` shares the suffix `ensa`, so a
longest-common-suffix walk reports the stem as `pi`. Every e→ie cell reports `pi`,
so it CLUSTERS correctly and passes a counting exercise — then prints a card that
says "pi". We generated the regular form as stem + ending, so the cut point is
known rather than inferred. Cutting there leaves two stems whose difference is a
real operation: pens→piens is "insert i at 1", identical across pensar's eight
irregular cells and across two tenses.

The result reads like a textbook. `pedir` is ONE fact covering eighteen cells
(present, preterite, both subjunctives, gerund). `poder` is three: o→ue in the
boot, o→u in the preterite, and the podr- future. `tener` is four stem facts plus
the tuve/tuvo endings.

"SHORTEST FORM WINS" WAS NOT SAFE, AND THE BROWSER-EQUIVALENT HERE WAS READING THE
OUTPUT. It is correct about clitics — `hablándole` carries the same code as
`hablando`, so tags cannot separate them and length can. It is wrong about bad
data, and 14% of lemma/cell pairs in this table carry more than one candidate:
Wiktionary lists both `tiene` and `tiée` as the third-person present of `tener`,
tagged identically. `tiée` is not a word and it is one character shorter, so the
rule printed it on a card for a top-twenty verb and invented a stem-fact to
explain it. Candidates are now costed against the regular paradigm — exact match
free, stem tweak cheap, unmatched ending expensive — which picks `tiene` (insert
one letter) over `tiée` (rewrite two), still picks `hablando` over `hablándole`,
and still keeps `hablaremos` and `hablara`, which the filter I proposed two
sessions ago would have deleted. It removed 25 spurious A1 facts.

ONE PASS, NOT ONE PER VERB. The first version asked the table per verb and each
ask walked all 132,741 forms — 167 million iterations against the graded list. The
aggregate test took 133 seconds and timed out, which is how it was found; on a
device it would merely have been slow for no reason, where nobody would have
looked. Inverted once into a memoised index, it is 189 ms and O(1) per verb.

Measured, and these are the curriculum: 63% of graded verbs are perfectly regular;
5,222 irregular cells collapse to 819 facts, 6.4x. Cards by scope — A1 132, A2 210,
B1 308, C2 846 — so "about 350" is right for a learner through B1.

Pattern cards are taught first, per the ordering decision: an exception is only an
exception against a rule already held, and A1 is the most irregular band in the
language because the commonest verbs are the irregular ones.

790 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

entry.title: feat(storage): writing_state becomes drill_state, so a second drill c…
entry.content:
feat(storage): writing_state becomes drill_state, so a second drill costs a prefix

Phase 6 needs per-item FSRS state for Spanish conjugation, which is the same shape
as handwriting in every respect that matters: not a deck word, merged by whole-card
ownership, feeding no streak and no budget. A second column would have meant a
second migration, a second merge, and a second entry in all three of the places
lib/storage/supabase.ts demands — and a third drill a third of each.

So the column is renamed and the KEYS carry the drill: w:好 for handwriting,
c:hablar:pres for conjugation. lib/drillState.ts owns the shared half; writingState
keeps the handwriting logic and goes on working in bare characters, because
drillView strips the prefix on the way in and drillWrite restores it on the way
out. The namespace stops at the storage boundary.

THE PREFIX IS NOT REDUNDANT TODAY AND WOULD BE EXPENSIVE LATER. The blob is
already per language, so nothing could collide right now: only Chinese has
handwriting and only Spanish will have conjugation. But hasHandwriting is a config
flag, not a law — Japanese is a KanjiVG build script away from wanting both, and
then 食 and 食べる:past share one flat namespace with nothing but luck keeping them
apart.

MIGRATED BY READING THE DATA, NOT BY A VERSION MARKER. Every key written before
this is a bare Han character, so parseDrillKey reads an unprefixed key as
handwriting and it is rewritten with its prefix on the next save. deckGloss.ts
documents at length why a marker is a trap: it gets written by a run whose result
was discarded, and the migration is then marked done having done nothing. SQL
could not have done it anyway — it would fix the cloud and leave every device's
localStorage.

0004 RENAMES rather than replaces, because handwriting progress already exists in
production and a drop-and-create would delete it silently. It is idempotent both
ways: it renames only if writing_state is there, then adds drill_state if not.

saveDrillCards writes one drill INTO the base rather than over it. That is the one
way a shared column could be worse than two — handwriting saving its own cards
over the whole entry would delete conjugation progress for that language, silently,
on every character practised. Tested.

Verified in a browser with a LEGACY deck: two characters practised under the old
srsly-writing-zh key, both scheduled to 2027, correctly read as "Nothing due"
rather than as never-practised. The old key is deliberately left in place — a read
is not the right place to destroy the only copy of something.

Also: the practice sheet's sequence hint now shows in normal mode too, on request.
Two rows carrying an identical gloss read as a glitch rather than as a compound
word deliberately broken into parts.

766 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

entry.title: feat(zh): a new character is taught before it is tested, and the hint…
entry.content:
feat(zh): a new character is taught before it is tested, and the hint ladder gets a bottom rung

LEARN BEFORE QUIZ. A character with no reviews used to drop you onto a square with
a grey outline and expect you to produce something you had never met — not a test,
a guessing game, where every stroke after the first wrong one is a guess about a
guess. It now opens in Learn: the strokes animate in order, Replay is free, and
"Got it, let me try" starts the graded quiz. Nothing is scheduled until real
strokes arrive, so the teaching costs the scheduler nothing.

That is also where the "play the whole animation" request belongs. As a button
inside the quiz next to a self-grade it is a free answer; before the quiz it is
simply how you meet a character.

THE LADDER'S BOTTOM RUNG. Under "Show me the next stroke" sits "Watch the whole
character — counts as Again". It replays everything and then RESTARTS THE SAME
CHARACTER rather than advancing, so the thing just watched is the thing
immediately drawn. Both rungs set usedHint, which gradeFromStrokes turns into
Again, so watching is never free. Deliberately not "grade Again and skip":
skipping records the failure and teaches nothing at the one moment the learner has
asked to be taught.

ANIMATION TIMING IS NOT THE LIBRARY DEFAULT, and this is probably the "not smooth"
report. hanzi-writer's delayBetweenStrokes defaults to 1000 ms — a full second of
motionless screen between every stroke. The median HSK character has 9 strokes and
the worst has 23, so the default spends 9 to 23 seconds mostly showing nothing,
and it does not read as deliberate, it reads as broken: you cannot tell a pause
from a hang. Now 260 ms, with strokeAnimationSpeed 1.25.

THE STATS RING STOPPED POPPING IN. MilestoneRing started `selected` at 0 and
waited for storage.getPrefs() — signed in, a Supabase round trip — so `row` stayed
null, `if (!row) return null` rendered NOTHING, and a second later the whole card
appeared and shoved Milestones down the page. The level is now seeded
synchronously off localStorage, exactly as app/page.tsx already does for the study
language and for exactly this reason, and the null case renders a same-footprint
skeleton instead of nothing. It shows no percentage: printing "0%" while loading
would be the same mistake in the other direction.

The practice sheet's row numbers are gone on request. The answer key keeps its
order and now says so.

Found while double-checking: both hint buttons stayed live after a card was
graded, so the bottom rung could cancel and restart a quiz for a review that was
already over, underneath a verdict describing it. doneRef always blocked the
second grade so nothing was miscounted, but the controls offered an action that
could not mean anything. It predates the ladder; the ladder made it visible.

Verified in a browser: a practised character goes straight to the quiz, a new one
opens in Learn with the ladder hidden, autoplay settles to Replay, "Got it" swaps
Learn's controls for the ladder, and "Watch the whole character" animates and
returns to a live quiz on the same character. Sheet rows carry no numbers in
either mode.

758 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

entry.title: feat(zh): 田字格 practice paper — paper does the practice, the screen do…
entry.content:
feat(zh): 田字格 practice paper — paper does the practice, the screen does the measurement

The answer to "let me practise on paper and mark myself correct". A self-grade
button beside a stroke-verified one writes a review the scheduler can never tell
apart from an observed one afterwards, so instead paper gets its own surface —
one that claims nothing. No FSRS write, no schedule, no streak, no heatmap, and
tests/practiceSheet.test.ts pins that by asserting this module cannot import
anything able to schedule.

window.print() AND NOT A PDF LIBRARY. jsPDF or pdfmake would have to draw 水
itself, which means embedding a CJK font — megabytes, to render characters we
already ship as vector outlines. The browser is the renderer, every print dialog
has Save as PDF including iOS Safari's share sheet, and one code path serves
print and PDF both.

THE CHARACTERS COME FROM public/strokes/, SO NO LIBRARY LOADS AT ALL. A stroke
file is plain SVG path strings, so drawing one needs a <path> and the vertical
flip; hanzi-writer's 36 kB chunk stays where it is. Two things follow that a font
could not give: the sheet and the quiz use the same glyphs, so they cannot
disagree about stroke forms, and the stroke-order build-up band becomes possible.

THREE NUMBERS ARE MEASURED RATHER THAN CHOSEN.

The glyph box: coordinates run x 12..1014 and y -100..888, so after the flip the
overflow is entirely at the BOTTOM by 100 units. An estimate of "about 50 all
round" was wrong in size and direction. A test walks all 2,663 files and asserts
nothing clips, and a control asserts half the slack WOULD clip — so it is
measuring the data rather than being generously large.

Line weights: every box shares one viewBox, so a stroke-width in units is a
different PHYSICAL line depending on the size it is drawn at. The 田字格
cross-hairs went out at 5 units — 0.07 mm, a quarter of a screen pixel — and the
defining feature of the paper was invisible. Weights are now stated in
millimetres and converted per box.

Column count: ten 18 mm cells fit both A4 and US Letter at a 12 mm margin, which
is why it is ten.

TWO THINGS FOUND BY LOOKING AT A RENDERED SHEET, neither visible in the code. The
cross-hairs above; and with the models hidden, 朋 and 友 both label from 朋友, so
a recall sheet printed two consecutive rows reading "péngyou · friend" and
accepted either answer for both. Rows are now numbered and say which character of
the word they want.

globals.css gains the app's first @media print block, and it deliberately breaks
this repo's "never hardcode colours" rule: paper has no theme, and a sheet printed
in ink or dusk mode would emit a black page. The exception is commented so it is
not tidied away later.

Verified in a browser: the grid, the build-up band and model/trace/blank cells all
render; recall mode leaks no character into the cells or the labels and every row
label is distinct; the answer key carries one glyph per row.

758 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

entry.title: fix(state): the two bugs that survived their own fix, and a Write-mod…
entry.content:
fix(state): the two bugs that survived their own fix, and a Write-mode dead end

The report was that 631f169 did not hold. It did not, and neither fix was an edge
case — both were wrong in the same way, having been written against the wrong
signal.

TOAST. The re-seed latched on the render where `language` changed. The new
language's deck arrives one or more renders LATER, because useVocabDeck has to
read storage first — so the guard was spent against the OUTGOING deck, and by the
time the incoming one landed the diff had nothing left protecting it. Its backstop
compared `loadSeq` across languages, and that counter is per-language: Chinese's
third load against Spanish's third load is two unrelated facts that are both 3.
The two effects are now one, keyed on the language and counter the ids were
RECORDED WITH, and gated on `deckLoaded` — the same fix Flashcards already carries.

TYPE ANSWERS. Declaring `typedRecall` on `UserPrefs` was necessary and not
sufficient: a type is erased at runtime, and the write path never changed.
`setTypedRecall` wrote to localStorage and stopped, so the field never once reached
the row — and `SupabaseStorage.getPrefs()` mirrors the cloud's prefs down over local
wholesale, which app/page.tsx triggers on every language change for the pool
activation. Toggle on, switch language, and the blob was replaced by a copy that had
never heard of the field. It is invisible signed OUT, because LocalStorage reads back
what it just wrote — which is why it survived a fix and was only ever seen live.

WRITE MODE HAD NO EXIT. `mode` outlives a language switch; the toggle is gated on
`hasHandwriting`. So Chinese → Write → Spanish left mode on 'write' with no control
rendered to leave it: "Nothing to write yet", and a reload was the only way out.

LAG. The deck could not paint until `syncDeckGlosses` had fetched the language's
dictionary — 7.98 MB for Chinese, 5.45 MB for Spanish — so a language switch waited
on a multi-megabyte download before showing anything. The gloss repair now runs
behind the paint. `pruneDeckToCurriculum` stays in front, because its whole job is
stopping an off-curriculum word flashing into a review surface on its way out.

Verified in a browser, signed out: four language switches, zero toasts, typed mode
still on. The control matters as much — adding 水 through the Vocab tab still fires
"Added 水 to your deck", so the test bites rather than having silenced the toast.
Chinese → Write → Spanish now lands on Spanish flashcards.

733 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

entry.title: feat(practice): typed recall asks one question now — meaning in, word…
entry.content:
feat(practice): typed recall asks one question now — meaning in, word out, your own IME

Pivots typed recall so all four languages behave identically: English meaning on
the front, the word typed on the back. Chinese and Japanese are entered with the
learner's own OS IME, so the answer is the characters rather than a romanisation.

WANAKANA IS GONE, and that is the pivot rather than a side effect. It rewrote the
input's value to turn romaji into kana as you typed — which with a real Japanese
keyboard means two things transforming the same keystrokes, fighting over every
character. The app no longer touches the field: no library, no binding, and
lib/typedAnswer.ts stays synchronous because every comparison left is a codepoint
operation. The dependency is uninstalled and lib/kana.ts deleted.

THE OLD ARGUMENT WAS NOT WRONG AND IS KEPT IN THE DOCS. Facing zh/ja forward —
character shown, reading typed — rested on a real measurement: a multi-character
HSK word has a median of ONE homophone in all of CC-CEDICT, so pinyin→characters
is near deterministic and typing 朋友 tests less than it looks. What it missed is
that producing a word from its meaning and choosing the right characters is what
writing Chinese on a keyboard actually is.

The `close` tier is now the FORGOTTEN-KEYBOARD tier, which is what makes the
pinyin and kana work worth keeping. Type `pengyou` with the IME off, or press
Enter on たべる before converting to 食べる, and that grades Good showing the right
form instead of a lapse. Toneless on the Chinese side deliberately, because
toneless pinyin is what an IME is driven with; for Japanese the realistic miss is
unconverted kana, not romaji, so no romaji table is needed at all.

A katakana loanword typed in hiragana lands there too — こーひー is not an
alternative spelling of コーヒー, it is the reading in the wrong script. My test
asserted `exact` for that and the test was wrong, not the grader.

The bespoke "I was actually right" override is removed: Again/Hard/Good/Easy are
already on screen and pressing Good does exactly what it did.

isComposing stays and is load-bearing — Enter during composition commits the IME
candidate and must not also submit; the input stays uncontrolled so React cannot
re-render mid-composition and drop the candidate window.

CLAUDE.md's typed-recall section rewritten rather than left contradicting the
code, which is the failure its own opening section calls out.

733 tests, lint and typecheck clean. Not yet driven in a browser with a real IME.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(practice): three state bugs — a discarded pref, a deck mistaken f…
entry.content:
fix(practice): three state bugs — a discarded pref, a deck mistaken for an addition, a rewound counter

TOGGLE AMNESIA IS NOT A LIFECYCLE BUG. `typedRecall` was written straight
into the `srsly-prefs` blob by lib/flashcardPrefs.ts without being a field on
`UserPrefs`, so it existed only in the LOCAL copy. `getPrefs()` mirrors the
cloud row down over local wholesale, and the cloud blob never carried it — so
the next read wiped it. `handleLanguageChange` calls `getPrefs()`, which is
exactly why switching language turned the toggle off and nothing else did.

A field the storage layer does not know about is a field it will discard.
Declaring it on UserPrefs is the whole fix. `reverseCards` was declared from
the start and never had this problem, which is why the two behaved differently
and made it look like an unmount issue.

THE "ADDED 711 WORDS" TOAST is the sixth failure mode in CLAUDE.md wearing a
new face. ToastHost re-seeds silently on `loadSeq`, which counts loads from
STORAGE and so covers signing in — but a language switch replaces the deck
wholesale, often from the in-memory cache with no load at all. The diff then
saw 711 unfamiliar ids and announced them as additions. Re-seeding on either
signal fixes it; the toast now fires only for words actually saved.

SESSION COUNTER continuity across a language switch, DERIVED rather than
stored: a card graded today already carries `lastReview === today`, so the
count of work done before this mount is a read over the deck, not a new
per-day counter that would drift the first time either was written alone.
Captured once at the queue latch so it keeps meaning "before this session",
with `results.length` carrying the rest. 3 of 34 no longer rewinds to 1 of 32.

743 tests, lint and typecheck clean. Not yet driven in a browser.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(zh): the writing canvas — draw the character, graded by its strokes
entry.content:
feat(zh): the writing canvas — draw the character, graded by its strokes

The frontend for Phase 5. A Cards/Write toggle in SrsTab, gated on the new
`hasHandwriting` config flag rather than a `language === 'zh'` check, opening a
drawing surface that grades what you drew and feeds lib/writingState.ts.

touch-action: none on the surface is the whole mobile story. hanzi-writer
listens for pointer moves and preventDefaults them, but the browser decides
whether a touch is a SCROLL before delivering any move event — so without that
one property a finger drag scrolls the page and the library receives almost
nothing. The feature would not work at all on the hardware it exists for.

The library has no destroy(): it appends an SVG to the host and leaves it, so
the cleanup clears the host by hand. Verified by advancing a card and counting —
one SVG before, one after, not two.

Colours resolve from CSS variables at runtime. hanzi-writer parses hex into
rgba and cannot read var(--ink), so its defaults would make this the one screen
that ignores all six themes; a MutationObserver on data-theme pushes changes
through updateColor so a mid-session theme switch is not stale until the next
character.

Lazily imported, and checked rather than asserted: the library lands in its own
36 kB chunk, and .next/app-build-manifest.json lists seven chunks for / and not
that one. Stroke data comes from srsly's own public/strokes/, never a CDN — a
CDN would make the feature depend on a third party being up and would leak which
characters a learner is practising to a host they never chose.

Typed against a five-method `WriterHandle` rather than `any`, so the dependency
surface is visible — including the one private field (`_quiz._currentStrokeIndex`)
the hint button needs, which now shows up as a type to update if upstream renames
it rather than as a hint that silently animates the wrong stroke.

VERIFIED BY DRIVING IT, not by reading it. Dispatching all 8 strokes of 朋 along
their real medians produced "Clean.", revealed the character and persisted
{"朋":{"phase":"learning","learningStep":1,...}} — scheduling fields only, no
gloss. And the firewall held in the running app: srsly-activity-log and
srsly-review-counts stayed null, srs_state kept todayScore 0 with empty sessions,
and no deck word gained a `reviews` or `dueAt`. Writing graded; reading untouched.

/ first-load JS is 305 kB, up from the 287 kB recorded before typed recall, the
phonetic series, the PWA and this — CLAUDE.md's figures updated to match rather
than left to drift.

743 tests, lint and typecheck clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(zh): handwriting foundation — stroke data, per-character schedul…
entry.content:
feat(zh): handwriting foundation — stroke data, per-character schedule, its own column

The data pipeline and schema for Phase 5. No UI yet: nothing in the app reaches
this code and the new column is written by nobody.

WHAT IS KEYED BY WHAT is the whole design. A deck card is a WORD; writing is a
character skill. 朋友 is one card and two things to learn to draw, and 朋 turns
up again in every other word the learner owns that contains it — so keyed by
word, one character's schedule would exist in as many copies as it has words and
they would disagree from the first review. Keyed by character it is also a
SMALLER set than the deck rather than a doubling of it: HSK's 4,991 words are
built from 2,663 distinct characters.

That is what forces the project's first schema change. A second FSRS block on
DeckWord would have been free — it lives inside the `decks` jsonb and the
on-load strip is a denylist — but it is the wrong key. Hence `writing_state`,
in UserDataRow, schema.sql and migrations/0003. Control-checked: removing it
from schema.sql fails tests/sync.test.ts by name.

IT FEEDS NOTHING ELSE, and a test pins that. Not isDueToday, not the reading
streak, not the daily budget, not the heatmap. Writing is a gym, not a daily
requirement, so being a month behind on it must never read as a broken reading
streak. The test strips comments first, because this module's prose names
isDueToday repeatedly to explain what it is walled off FROM — a raw substring
check would fail on the documentation and push the next person to delete the
explanation to get CI green.

A card is owned WHOLE on merge. Stability, difficulty, lapses and due date
describe one review history, so a per-field max composes a state neither device
was ever in — the argument srsStateMerge makes about the streak. Ties fall
through to canonical JSON order because the rule must be COMMUTATIVE, not just
deterministic: a device writes its merged copy back, so "mine wins ties" makes
two devices ping-pong for ever, invisibly from either one.

CHINESE ONLY, for data honesty rather than scope. Measured: 88.7% of JLPT kanji
appear in hanzi-writer-data, but the 223 missing are exactly the shinjitai
(厳倹権鉱渉沢団読売楽児発), and among those present are characters whose Japanese
stroke order differs (直, 令, 骨). It would teach confidently wrong stroke order
for a subset nobody could identify. hanzi-writer-data-jp is not the answer
either — experimental, and its npm package ships no data files at all.

One file per character rather than one bundle, which breaks this repo's usual
rule deliberately: a session practises a handful of characters, so ~2.4 kB each
means ~48 kB against 1.41 MB for a level shard and 7.00 MB for the lot. The cost
is 2,663 files — identical bytes, worse file count.

The Arphic Public License is an obligation, not a footnote: ARPHICPL.TXT travels
verbatim (§1), and because subsetting DELETES characters from the glyph table,
MODIFICATIONS.txt states what changed and when (§2a) with the build script
reproducing it exactly (§2b). Nothing inside a character file is touched.

fsrsSchedule now takes a `Schedulable` rather than a whole DeckWord — it only
ever read the scheduling fields, and requiring a word meant a character card
would have had to invent a gloss to satisfy a type. DeckWord satisfies the
narrower type structurally, so no caller changed.

743 tests (+27), lint and typecheck clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(practice): type the answer, and ask each language what it can ac…
entry.content:
feat(practice): type the answer, and ask each language what it can actually test

Typed recall as a toggle on the existing flashcard — no new tab, no new card
type, no schema change, gradeCard untouched.

The mode is NOT one exercise in four languages. Spanish and French have
`hasReadings: false`, so their forward card has nothing to type and the
exercise is meaning → word. Chinese and Japanese cannot be typed at all
without an IME handing over the characters, so theirs is word → reading.
Opposite orientations, decided by the flag that already encodes the
difference rather than by a new one.

Typing therefore PINS the orientation and disables Flip. That is a
correctness fix: reverse + typed in Chinese asks "the word for friend?" and
demands one romanisation, so a learner answering with another correct word
takes a real FSRS lapse for a card they knew.

wanakana (MIT, 21 kB, lazily imported) converts romaji on the INPUT and is
never used for grading, because measuring it showed it disagrees with itself:
`toHiragana('コーヒー')` is こうひい while typing `ko-hi-` gives こーひー, across
the 10.4% of JMdict readings written in katakana. The grader shifts codepoints
and resolves ー to the vowel it lengthens, one rule on both sides — so it stays
synchronous, mock-free, and out of every Spanish learner's bundle. The input's
IME mode is chosen from the answer's own script, which is what makes `ko-hi-`
land on コーヒー exactly.

Three tiers. `close` is "right skeleton, wrong layer on top" — tone, accent,
sloppy kana — and grades Good showing the correct form. Marks that carry a
contrast are not folded: ü (女 nǚ ≠ 努 nǔ) and ñ (año ≠ ano). ç is folded,
since no French pair turns on a cedilla. A doubled vowel is never collapsed:
おばさん and おばあさん are different words.

The "I was actually right" override is es/fr only, where synonyms make the
question genuinely ambiguous. zh/ja ask for this card's reading, which is
determined; a polyphone gets a sentence naming the reading they hit instead.

A card with no stored pinyin is not typed at all — grading an absent answer
marks the learner wrong for a hole in our data. Audio hides until reveal in
typed mode, or every zh/ja card was solvable by pressing play.

Verified in a browser, not just compiled: `ko-hi-` → コーヒー and `taberu` →
たべる live, per-card IME mode, Flip disabled, `ano` for `año` graded wrong,
the polyphone line, the override advancing the card, and the answer panel
measured at height 0 before reveal.

Extracted `stripTones` and `canonPinyin` in lib/pinyin.ts so phoneticSeries
and this share one ü-preserving implementation; `u:`/`v` now normalise before
tone marks are applied, which is what `lu:4` needed.

716 tests (+29), lint and typecheck clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(pwa): installable on a phone, an iPad and a desktop
entry.content:
feat(pwa): installable on a phone, an iPad and a desktop

Until now srsly was a website that happened to work on a phone: no home-screen
icon, no standalone window, no way in without typing a URL into a browser. For
a spaced-repetition app that gap is bigger than it sounds, because reviews
happen in dead minutes — a queue, a lift, a bus — which is exactly when nobody
is going to type a URL.

`app/manifest.ts` plus the iOS metadata Next does not put in the manifest. The
icon is the app's OWN vocabulary rather than a new mark: accent ground, paper
strokes, and the `page` glyph already used in ReadingSources. Geometry, not a
character and not an emoji, for the reason BadgeSeal gives — the app is four
languages and its icon is about none of them. SVG for everything that takes one,
with a 192px PNG because iOS home-screen icons do not.

The three literal colours in the manifest are the one place in this codebase a
hardcoded colour is correct rather than a slip: a manifest is JSON handed to the
operating system and cannot read a CSS variable. They are the existing --accent
and --paper values, not new ones.

Verified served rather than merely compiled: /manifest.webmanifest linked and
parsing, display standalone, both icons 200, apple-touch-icon set, theme-color
matching the manifest. Next 15 emits `mobile-web-app-capable` rather than the
`apple-` prefixed name — that is the modern standard Apple moved to in iOS 16.4,
not a missing tag.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT YET DO IS WORK OFFLINE. Installable and offline-capable are
separate things: without a service worker, opening it without signal still shows
the browser's offline page. The data layer is already built for it — the write
queue, the read guards, localStorage — so the missing piece is only the app
shell. That is deliberately not in this commit, because a caching strategy that
gets it wrong serves stale JavaScript and is far harder to notice than a missing
icon.

Also removed five create-next-app SVGs from public/ — file, globe, next, vercel
and window — confirmed unreferenced by anything in the repo.

entry.title: feat(zh): the popup says which part gives the sound, and how far to t…
entry.content:
feat(zh): the popup says which part gives the sound, and how far to trust it

One line under the decomposition: the phonetic, three worked examples, and the
family's own verdict. 艮 blunt → only 7 of 11 sound alike — 恨 hèn · 眼 yǎn ·
退 tuì. 己 self → sounds like 岂 qǐ · 忌 jì · 纪 jì · 4 of 5.

This answers a question the component previously could not. SOUND / MEANING tags
on the components were tried here before and removed, because "孝 filial piety
SOUND" invites "sound of what?" and answers nothing. Naming the family and its
measured reading is what finally answers it.

TWO BUGS, BOTH FOUND BY OPENING THE POPUP RATHER THAN READING THE CODE.

The sample excluded the looked-up character AFTER clustering, which deleted a
cluster's only representative: 很 is first in 艮's largest group, so the line
showed 眼 yǎn and 退 tuì — two singletons — and a family where 7 of 11 share
"-en" rendered as pure noise. Excluding before clustering fixes it, and
tests/phoneticSeries.test.ts now pins that the first example still speaks for the
biggest group.

And the low end read "no single sound", which is often false. 艮 has a real
majority on "-en" that simply does not clear the bar; flatly denying a pattern
visible in the examples below teaches the learner to distrust the label rather
than the phonetic. It now says "only 7 of 11 sound alike", which is calibrated
and needs no second threshold.

The index is memoised, and it REFUSES TO CACHE AN EMPTY ANSWER: readings come
from cedict, which loads asynchronously, so a call before it lands builds an
empty index — and caching that would freeze "there are no phonetic families" for
the session, silently, on the first render. That is CLAUDE.md's sixth failure
mode exactly, and the guard is two lines.

Layout holds: the line uses the same nowrap + overflow-x pattern as the equation
above it, so a long row scrolls inside itself; verified the page does not scroll
sideways with the popup open.

Also verified, and it makes an earlier claim of mine wrong: the app ALREADY
teaches ü input. `readingHelp` for Chinese reads "(lv4 for lǜ · no number =
neutral tone e.g. le)" directly above the pinyin field, and toneNumToMark
converts lv4 → lǜ and nv3 → nǚ. `u:` is not accepted, which is the notation
CC-CEDICT uses raw; srsly's own copy is already tone-marked, so nothing reaches
a learner that way. No change made — there was no gap to fix.

entry.title: feat(zh): choose the examples to argue the family's own verdict
entry.content:
feat(zh): choose the examples to argue the family's own verdict

The display sampler, and the cap is the easy half of it.

Fourteen members of 者 in a popup is a wall of text at the moment the learner is
already working hard, so it is capped at three. What it is capped TO matters
more. Frequency ordering is the obvious rule and teaches the wrong thing: on an
unreliable family it would cheerfully pick three members that happen to agree,
demonstrating a regularity that is not there and contradicting the verdict
printed beside it.

So the sample argues the actual case. A predictive family shows its modal
cluster — the shared sound becomes the visible pattern. An unreliable one shows
one member from each of its largest clusters — the DISAGREEMENT becomes the
visible pattern. Tested both ways round: 青's three examples all match its modal
reading, 者's three all differ from each other.

This is also where the tone caveat lives, and it is deliberately not a sentence.
The members print with their real tone marks side by side — 清 qīng · 情 qíng ·
请 qǐng — so three tones on one shared syllable are adjacent and unmissable. A
disclaimer would be read past. Colour-coding the tones was considered and
rejected: it carries the point in hue alone, which fails a colour-blind reader,
and it would have to survive six themes to say something the tone marks on
screen already say.

Note for the UI: SOUND / MEANING tags on components were tried here before and
removed, because "孝 filial piety SOUND" invites "sound of what?" and answers
nothing. Naming the family and its shared sound is what can finally answer that,
which is the whole reason this measurement was worth taking.

entry.title: feat(zh): phonetic series, scored for reliability rather than assumed
entry.content:
feat(zh): phonetic series, scored for reliability rather than assumed

青 gives the sound, 氵忄讠 give the meaning. han-decomp.json has held that all
along — every pictophonetic entry carries `ph` and `se` — so the feature needed
no new data. What it needed was a measurement.

HAVING THE DATA IS NOT THE SAME AS THE DATA BEING TRUE. 2,097 characters carry a
phonetic component; only a fraction of those components predict anything.
Measured against cedict's own readings, the BIGGEST family in the set is the
worst: 者, 14 members, splitting 猪诸著渚煮箸 zhu / 堵睹赌 du / 暑署 shu / 奢 she
/ 绪 xu / 都 dou. 隹 has nine members and nine readings. Shipping every series as
predictive would have taught wrong guesses at scale.

Three things the scoring had to get right, each of which was wrong first:

  SELF-AGREEMENT, NOT COMPONENT-MATCHING. "Does it read like 青?" reports 0% for
  长 → 帐张胀账, which are unanimously zhāng. The shared sound is the lesson; the
  component is only the hook.

  MODAL SHARE, NOT UNANIMITY. Requiring every member to agree is a size filter in
  disguise — every unanimous family had 3–5 members and no larger one passed. It
  also excluded 青 itself (清情请晴 qing, 睛精 jing, 猜 cai), i.e. the textbook
  example of the thing being taught.

  PAIRWISE TOLERANCE, NEVER TRANSITIVE. j/q/x came from g/k/h and from z/c/s
  before front vowels, so qing/jing is one sound change and 青 scores 86% once
  that is allowed. But the pairs CHAIN: retroflex ↔ sibilant ↔ palatal ↔ velar,
  so unioning them into equivalence classes makes every sibilant and velar in
  Mandarin mutually tolerant and the threshold stops filtering.

That last failure is silent, which is why the numbers are pinned. Reverting to a
transitive implementation moves the golden test from 91 families / 379 chars to
92 / 385 — one family, six characters. It would have read as noise. The test
asserts the pair `zh`/`g` is not tolerant, and the golden count catches the rest.

Reliability is a PROPERTY, never an admission ticket: 者 shown as three labelled
clusters teaches the thing this feature exists to prevent, which is trusting a
phonetic too far. Tone is never predicted — 妈麻马骂 — and the UI must say so.

91 predictive families, 379 characters, 344 of them (91%) in HSK 1–6.

entry.title: feat(settings): four groups, and Speech covers every language you study
entry.content:
feat(settings): four groups, and Speech covers every language you study

Two things reported together, both about the same page having outgrown itself.

SPEECH WAS STUCK ON THE STUDY LANGUAGE. It read `useLanguage()`, so someone
studying four could only ever set the voice for the one currently selected, and
the section announced "How Chinese is read aloud" with no hint the other three
had their own. A voice is per language by nature — a French voice cannot read
Chinese — so the section now carries its own selector over the added languages.
Speed is unchanged and stays global, because a multiplier means the same thing
in every language; its caption said otherwise and now does not.

The preview had a real bug behind that: `speak()` resolves its voice from the
module's `currentLocale`, which the app sets from the STUDY language — so
auditioning French while studying Chinese would have read French text through a
Chinese voice and the picker would have looked broken. The locale is pushed for
the preview and restored on the way out.

TEN SECTIONS IN ONE SCROLL is a list to be endured: the only route to a daily
limit ran past the level table, the voice picker and the retention dial. Four
groups — Account, Studying, Scheduling, Backup — declared once and read twice, as
the nav and as the render gate, so a group cannot exist in one and not the other.
Nothing is hidden that was not already several screens down.

Also added the line that would have saved a round trip today: a voice downloaded
after the browser started is genuinely absent from the list rather than filtered
out of it, because browsers enumerate system voices once at startup.

Verified with two languages added:

              Scheduling → retention · max interval · pool · daily limits
              Account → account · languages
  speech      chips Chinese/French; zh lists Tingting·Meijia·Li-Mu,
              fr lists Thomas·Marie·Amélie
  preview     zh-CN spoke Chinese as Yu-shu; fr-FR spoke French as Thomas

entry.title: feat(settings): choose the voice and the speed
entry.content:
feat(settings): choose the voice and the speed

Both were fixed constants — the voice came from a hand-ranked priority list, the
speed from a per-language table — and the ranking is a good default and a bad
only-option. It can only pick from what this machine happens to have installed,
and quality across system voices varies more than anything else in the audio
path. Dictation made that matter: skimming a passage tolerates a robotic voice,
straining to catch a word does not.

THEY ARE STORED APART, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN. Speed is a preference and syncs
in `prefs.ttsSpeed`; 0.8 means the same thing on every device. Voice is a fact
about the MACHINE and stays device-local in `srsly-tts-voice`, because voices are
installed per device — a voiceURI from a Mac with the enhanced Chinese voices
downloaded does not exist on a phone, so syncing it would push a choice onto a
device that cannot honour it and the silent fallback would look like the setting
being broken. Same reasoning that keeps the Anthropic key out of the blob.

Speed is a MULTIPLIER rather than an absolute rate. `RATE` is calibrated per
language — Chinese slowest, because tone contours are what a beginner strains to
hear — and one absolute number would flatten that, making one language sluggish
to make another intelligible.

Three smaller decisions, all in CLAUDE.md: a chosen voice outranks the novelty
filter (someone who picked Zarvox has answered the question the filter was
guessing at) but is still matched against the installed list, so an uninstalled
one falls through rather than silencing the app; `clearVoiceCache()` exists
because the resolved voice is cached by LOCALE and picking a new voice does not
change the locale; and the picker deduplicates, because the priority names are
substring matches and several nest — `Google 普通话（中国大陆）` and `Google 普通话`
are both satisfied by one installed voice, which listed it twice.

Verified in a browser against the real voice list, not assumed:
  picker lists  Tingting · Meijia · Li-Mu · Sinji · Yu-shu   (no duplicate)
  default       spoke as Tingting, the ranking's own choice
  after picking spoke as Yu-shu on the very next preview
  speed 1.4×    spoke at 1.148 = 0.82 × 1.4, calibration intact

A caution worth recording for later: do NOT fix the audio by setting
OPENAI_API_KEY in production. `consumeAiCredit` rations generation per guest;
/api/tts has no budget check at all, so any anonymous visitor could spend the
operator's credit by pressing play. Bring-your-own-key is the route there.

entry.title: feat(read): listening dictation — the cloze passage with the text wit…
entry.content:
feat(read): listening dictation — the cloze passage with the text withheld

Phase 3. A Listen toggle on a generated passage plays each sentence whole,
hides the text, and lets the learner type into the blanks that were already
there.

THE REFRAME IS THE WHOLE DESIGN: this is a presentation, not a second exercise.
The blanks, the typed input, the grading and the FSRS write are all what
ClozeBlank already does; only what can be SEEN changes. No new stored state, no
schema change, and a heard blank grades as a read one — recognising by ear is
arguably harder, but a second scale would be a second record of one fact.

`speakWithBlank()` was the planned entry point and is the wrong tool. It speaks
up to the blank, goes silent, then speaks the rest — so the learner never hears
the word they are asked to type, and "type what you heard" needs it spoken. The
audio is complete here and the TEXT is what has gaps. It also takes exactly one
gap while a sentence can carry several, since a word is blanked in all of its
occurrences and blanks have no ceiling. It keeps a real job as the "With the
gap" hint, for someone who has heard the sentence and still cannot place the
word.

Four things worth knowing, all in CLAUDE.md:
  - SRS only. Own reading commits vocabWords: [] and has no blanks to dictate.
  - A sentence reveals the moment its last blank is answered. One with no blanks
    is never hidden — nothing could ever earn it.
  - A hidden token is masked plain text, not a blurred TokenEl: blurring the
    real thing leaves it tappable and the popup would print the answer.
  - Hints forced off while dictating; they give live per-character feedback.

PassageText's "is this occurrence a blank" rule is now computed once instead of
inline in the token loop — dictation needs it per sentence, and two copies of a
rule that already handles Japanese base forms and already-graded occurrences is
how they come to disagree.

Verified in a browser: 4 sentences → 3 stops (the one with no blanks is not a
stop and is not hidden); answering sentence one dropped it from 10 blurred
tokens to 0 while 9 and 5 stayed hidden; the transport steps and disables at the
ends; the Read tab offers no Listen control at all.

660 tests, 10 of them new for the pure half.

entry.title: fix(sync): prefs and srs_state merge per field instead of overwriting…
entry.content:
fix(sync): prefs and srs_state merge per field instead of overwriting whole

The last of the three defects Phase 2 was for, and the one CLAUDE.md named as
unfixed: both columns were written as ONE BLOB, last-writer-wins. Every field
travelled with every save, so a device holding a stale copy reverted the whole
column on its next write — change the theme on a phone and the laptop's level
goes back; open the phone after studying on the laptop and the streak walks
backwards. Nothing errors, and a setting that quietly returns to a value you did
once choose is close to undetectable.

THE STREAK IS OWNED, NOT MAXIMISED, and that is the part worth reading. MAX is
the reflex and it is right for the counters and wrong for the streak, because a
streak is allowed to go DOWN: break it and it resets to 1, which no per-field
maximum can represent — a stale 40 would resurrect a streak already lost. That
is the mirror of the bug being fixed and strictly worse, since it inflates. The
streak instead belongs to whichever side has the later `lastActive`, which is
already the authoritative last-studied day, and the two travel together: a count
from one device beside a date from the other is a state neither was ever in.

`prefs` are choices rather than tallies, so no max or union means anything for a
theme. They take a THREE-WAY merge against the last value this device saw in the
cloud, applying only the fields that differ from that base — knowing what the
device CHANGED rather than what it holds is the entire bug. With no base, `mine`
wins the scalars, which is the old behaviour kept as the floor. Four keyed
collections merge per key regardless, because losing an entry there does real
damage: `poolAutoDate` (dropping one reintroduces the double-activation
avalanche it was moved into prefs to prevent), `testedLevels`, `placementSeen`,
`languages`.

`canonicalJson` moves to its own module; prefs needs it to ask "did this device
change this field?" of values that are objects, and a JSONB round trip does not
preserve key order.

32 tests: the two merges, plus tests/blobMergeWiring.test.ts asserting the
PAYLOAD rather than the functions — the wiring is the half that can silently
regress, since these were one-line blob writes and an edit could make them one
again without failing a merge test. Against the pre-fix writes it fails on
exactly the three harms CLAUDE.md described: 9 sent over 10, level 3 over 5, and
{zh:4} losing {es:2}.

docs: CLAUDE.md had gone stale within a day of the UI changing

Three corrections and one addition.

The empty Read tab is described as four cards led by a starter text and badged
with a key emoji. It has been two cards, no starter text and no emoji since
2026-09-04 — changes made a few hours before this. The file's own opening exists
because of exactly this failure (the ts-fsrs and SvelteKit leftovers that
"contradicted the code they were meant to describe"), so a fresh contradiction
in the first section a reviewer reads is the worst place to leave one.

`ReadingSources` was also described as collapsed to "+ Add reading" in EVERY
state including the empty tab. That decision was reverted — the component's own
docstring records why — and it lists lyrics as a third source, which has no
component in the tree at all.

The flaky list gains a sixth entry, because four separate bug reports in one day
turned out to be one mistake: a loading state rendered as an answer. A skeleton
and a "writing your passage" caption while only reading the cache; "Nothing to
review yet" to someone holding 542 words; "Added 542 words" on sign-in. In each,
a value meaning "not here yet" was rendered as "there is none", and the flag to
separate them already existed. Its corollary is worth as much: three of the four
would not reproduce locally, because LocalStorage answers before React can paint
and these only exist once the data crosses a network.

And the storage section now records the 52-queries-per-load measurement and why
sharing an in-flight fetch does not weaken the freshness rule it sits under.

Still stale and NOT touched here, because I have not established whether the
feature was removed deliberately: the "No songs ship with the app" paragraph
describes a listen-along panel and an .lrc helper block, and no such component
exists.
